etymology: Of uncertain first root, probably a blending of the Old English tergan (“to vex, to delay”) with the Old French targer, “to delay, to linger,” from a Late Latin tardicare, from tardus, “slow”; hence to stay, to abide, to wait, to put off going.
biblical_def: To tarry is to stay, to abide in a place, to wait rather than go — and in Scripture it is almost always a command laid upon impatient men. Boaz bids Ruth, “Tarry this night” (Rut 3:13), and the waiting woman receives a kinsman-redeemer in the morning. The risen Christ, before He ascended, “commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father” (Act 1:4), and the church that tarried ten days in one accord was clothed with power at Pentecost. Habakkuk is given the great rule of the waiting saint: “though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry” (Hab 2:3) — the vision seems slow to the flesh and is never late to God. But the word’s deepest note sounds in Gethsemane, where the Man of Sorrows, whose soul was exceeding sorrowful even unto death, asked of His three, “tarry ye here, and watch with me” (Mat 26:38) — and they slept. Christ tarried in the garden and drank the cup; His disciples could not tarry one hour. So the word divides the flesh from the Spirit. To tarry is not idleness but obedience: it is the creature refusing to run before his God, holding his post until the word comes. The Lord who bade His own tarry for the Spirit bids His church tarry still, watching for His appearing, since He that shall come will come, and will not tarry.
webster_summary: To stay; to abide; to wait; to delay going or coming; to linger in expectation.
webster_full: TARRY, to stay; to abide; to continue in a place.
To wait; to delay going, in expectation of another’s coming or command.
To be slow in coming, as a vision or a promise long deferred (Hab 2:3).
Christ commanded the disciples to tarry in Jerusalem for the Spirit (Act 1:4).
In Gethsemane, to tarry and watch with Christ was the charge the three failed (Mat 26:38).
scriptures: Then saith he unto them, My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me.
Act 1:4
And, being assembled together with them, commanded them that they should not depart from Jerusalem, but wait for the promise of the Father, which, saith he, ye have heard of me.
Hab 2:3
For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.
Rut 3:13

Tarry this night, and it shall be in the morning, that if he will perform unto thee the part of a kinsman, well; let him do the kinsman's part: but if he will not do the part of a kinsman to thee, then will I do the part of a kinsman to thee, as the LORD liveth: lie down until the morning.
corruption_summary: A plain word for waiting, and one the age can hardly bear: it recovers the obedience of the saint who will not run before his God.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live misuse here, and it is the impatience of a generation that will not wait for anything. The flesh reckons every delay a denial and every silence a refusal; it must have the answer now, the harvest now, the vision now, and it calls the God who bids it tarry slow. Habakkuk was taught otherwise: though the vision tarry, wait for it, for it will surely come and will not tarry. What seems slow to the creature is exactly punctual with the Creator, who has appointed the time and will not be hurried by our fretting. To tarry is not to do nothing; it is to hold the post until the word comes.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that waiting is a work of obedience, and Gethsemane is its measure. Christ, whose soul was exceeding sorrowful even unto death, asked no great labour of His three — only that they tarry and watch with Him — and they slept while He sweat as it were great drops of blood. The disciples who could not tarry one hour in the garden tarried ten days in the upper room after His command, and were filled with the Spirit. So the LORD teaches His own to stay where He sets them, watching for His appearing, since He that shall come will come and will not tarry.
roots_summary: The word means to stay, to abide, to wait, to delay going.
roots_lines: Tarry — probably Old English tergan blended with Old French targer, “to delay.”
Behind it stands the Latin tardus, “slow.”
It denotes staying, abiding, waiting rather than going.
Christ bade the disciples tarry for the promise of the Father (Act 1:4).
Though the vision tarry, wait for it: it will not tarry past its hour (Hab 2:3).
usage: Tarry ye here, and watch with me — the lightest charge of Gethsemane, and the three could not keep it.
The church tarried in Jerusalem till she was clothed with power; obedience waited, and Pentecost came.
Though it tarry, wait for it: what is slow to the flesh is punctual with God.

etymology: From the Middle English doten, “to be silly, to act foolishly,” kin to the Middle Dutch doten, “to be crazed”; hence to be weak-minded or foolish, and thence to love to excess and without judgment — the wits gone out after the thing loved.
biblical_def: To dote is to be silly, foolish, out of one’s wits — and so to love a thing beyond reason, the mind emptied out after the object of desire. The KJV keeps both edges of the word. Jeremiah pronounces the LORD’s sword upon Babylon: “A sword is upon the liars; and they shall dote” (Jer 50:36). Her wise men and diviners, who had counselled a proud empire, are struck with folly; God’s judgment on a nation of lies is to unmake its wisdom, so that the sages babble like idiots in the day of visitation. Ezekiel uses the other edge, and it cuts deeper. Aholah “played the harlot when she was mine; and she doted on her lovers, on the Assyrians her neighbours” (Eze 23:5), and again, “She doted upon the Assyrians… clothed most gorgeously, horsemen riding upon horses, all of them desirable young men” (Eze 23:12). Here doting is spiritual adultery: the covenant people, wedded to the LORD, gone silly after the gorgeous idols of the nations. Idolatry is not merely wicked; it is stupid, a bride losing her senses over a painted stranger. Paul brings the word into the church, and it lands on the proud teacher who is “doting about questions and strifes of words” (1Ti 6:4) — a man diseased with disputation, knowing nothing while he fancies himself wise. So Scripture names the whole ruin: to dote on idols, on lovers, on wrangling words, is the mind gone out of a man who has turned from God.
webster_summary: To be silly or weak-minded; and so to love to excess, the judgment overthrown by the thing loved.
webster_full: DOTE, to be delirious; to have the intellect impaired; to act foolishly.
To love to excess; to be foolishly fond, the judgment overthrown by the affection.
God’s judgment on the liars of Babylon was that they should dote (Jer 50:36).
In Ezekiel, to dote upon lovers is spiritual adultery against the LORD (Eze 23:5).
In Paul, a proud man may be sick with doting about questions and strifes of words (1Ti 6:4).
scriptures: A sword is upon the liars; and they shall dote: a sword is upon her mighty men; and they shall be dismayed.
He is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings,
Eze 23:5
And Aholah played the harlot when she was mine; and she doted on her lovers, on the Assyrians her neighbours,
She doted upon the Assyrians her neighbours, captains and rulers clothed most gorgeously, horsemen riding upon horses, all of them desirable young men.
corruption_summary: The old word names an excessive love that unmakes the mind; it recovers the truth that idolatry is not only wicked but witless.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live misuse here, for the age has made doting a virtue. To be wholly given over to a passion, to lose the head over a lover, a pleasure, a cause, is now praised as authenticity and depth of feeling — and Scripture calls it what it is: silliness, the intellect impaired by the thing desired. Ezekiel’s Aholah doted upon the Assyrians, gorgeous horsemen, desirable young men, and forsook the Husband who had betrothed her to Himself. An affection that will not be governed by the law of God is not a great love; it is a great folly, and it ends in the day of visitation with a sword upon the liars.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that idolatry is stupid before it is anything else — a rational creature emptying out his wits after a thing that cannot save. God’s judgment on Babylon’s wise men was to make them dote: the sages who lied for a living were struck with the folly they had loved. And the same word falls inside the church upon the man “proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words.” A soul may dote upon a wrangle as surely as upon an idol. Only a heart wedded to Christ and governed by His Word keeps its senses; every other love makes fools.
roots_summary: The word means to be silly or weak-minded, and so to love to excess without judgment.
roots_lines: Dote — Middle English doten, “to be silly, to act foolishly.”
Kin to the Middle Dutch doten, “to be crazed.”
It denotes the mind impaired, and thence a love beyond all reason.
To dote upon lovers is spiritual adultery against the LORD (Eze 23:5).
To dote about questions is the disease of the proud disputer (1Ti 6:4).
usage: A sword is upon the liars, and they shall dote: God unmakes the wisdom of a lying nation.
Aholah doted on gorgeous strangers and forsook her Husband — idolatry is a bride gone silly.
The proud teacher dotes about questions, sick with disputing, and knows nothing at all.

etymology: From the Old French dissimuler, from the Latin dissimulare, “to make unlike, to disguise, to feign that a thing is not what it is” (from dis-, “not,” and similis, “like”); hence to hide under a false appearance, to play the part of what one is not.
biblical_def: To dissemble is to disguise the truth by acting a part — not the blunt lie of the mouth only, but the lie of the whole man, the false face that makes a thing seem what it is not. Achan’s theft is charged so: Israel “have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff” (Jos 7:11). The wedge of gold hid in the tent was covered by a face that stood among the tribes as though nothing were amiss. Solomon marks the same craft in speech: “He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him” (Pro 26:24) — hatred is smooth outside and stores its poison within. The word’s gravest hour is at Antioch. Peter, who had eaten freely with the Gentiles, withdrew when certain came from James, fearing them of the circumcision; “and the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation” (Gal 2:13). Not one word of false doctrine was preached — only a chair moved, a table left — yet the act denied justification by faith alone, and the contagion carried off even Barnabas. So Paul “withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed” (Gal 2:11), publicly, before them all. Here is the rule the church must keep: where the truth of the gospel is at stake, the apostle would not spare an apostle. Dissembling is never a small thing, for it preaches with the body what the mouth would never dare say.
webster_summary: To hide under a false appearance; to feign; to act a part contrary to the truth of the thing.
webster_full: DISSEMBLE, to hide under a false appearance; to conceal the real fact or motive.
From the Latin dissimulare, “to make unlike, to feign.”
Achan stole and dissembled, the false face covering the accursed thing (Jos 7:11).
He that hateth dissembleth with his lips and layeth up deceit within (Pro 26:24).
At Antioch Peter and the Jews dissembled, and even Barnabas was carried away (Gal 2:13).
scriptures: Gal 2:11
But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed.
Gal 2:13
And the other Jews dissembled likewise with him; insomuch that Barnabas also was carried away with their dissimulation.
Jos 7:11

Israel hath sinned, and they have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them: for they have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff.
He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him;
corruption_summary: A live and pressing corruption: the age calls dissembling kindness, and a winsome cowardice that will not name error is Antioch over again.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not in the word but in our practice of the thing, and it wears a pleasant name. Peter at Antioch preached no heresy; he simply withdrew from the Gentile table when the men of the circumcision came in, and by that quiet courtesy he denied with his feet the gospel he had confessed with his mouth. Our own dissembling is the same: the minister who will not say from the pulpit what he believes in the study, the man who softens the doctrine to keep the room warm, the church that calls its silence winsomeness. It is dissimulation, and Barnabas himself — the son of consolation, Paul’s own companion — was carried away with it. Cowardice in the pulpit is contagious; it never stops with the coward.

Paul’s answer is the standing rule: he “withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed,” and he did it before them all. Gospel clarity outranks ecclesiastical politeness. Where justification by faith alone is at stake, the deference owed to a great name is owed no longer, for the truth of the gospel is not Peter’s property nor Paul’s but Christ’s. Achan’s dissembling hid a wedge of gold and cost Israel a battle and a valley of trouble; the dissembling at Antioch would have hidden the cross itself. Better an open rebuke that saves the church than a smooth face that damns it, for he that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and he that loves speaks plainly.
roots_summary: The word means to hide the truth under a false appearance, to feign what one is not.
roots_lines: Dissemble — Old French dissimuler, from Latin dissimulare.
From dis-, “not,” and similis, “like” — to make a thing unlike itself.
It denotes the lie of the whole man, not of the tongue only.
Achan stole and dissembled, hiding the accursed thing (Jos 7:11).
Peter’s dissimulation at Antioch drew Paul’s open rebuke (Gal 2:11-13).
usage: Achan dissembled: the wedge lay in the tent while his face stood innocent among the tribes.
Peter dissembled at Antioch by moving a chair, and denied with his feet what he confessed with his lips.
Paul withstood him to the face — gospel clarity outranks every politeness owed to a great name.

etymology: The archaic third-person form of wink, from the Old English wincian, “to close the eyes, to blink”; in the KJV it names the sly closing of one eye as a signal of mischief between confederates, and thence any wicked hint given without a word.
biblical_def: To wink, in the Authorized Version, is not the harmless blink of the eye but the signal of a conspirator — the eye that says what the mouth is too cunning to speak. Solomon draws the whole man: “A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth” (Pro 6:12), and then, “He winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers” (Pro 6:13). Every member is enlisted in the mischief; the body has become a language of wickedness, and not one word of it can be brought into court. This is sin grown expert — the shared glance across a room, the nudge that recruits a fellow-sinner without ever committing the speaker to anything. The LORD hates it: the six things He hates and the seven that are an abomination follow immediately upon that portrait. Again Solomon warns, “He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow: but a prating fool shall fall” (Pro 10:10) — the sly man and the loud man are set side by side, and both come to ruin; the one sows grief by silence, the other by noise. David prays against the same eye: “neither let them wink with the eye that hate me without a cause” (Psa 35:19), the causeless hater signalling his malice in triumph. So the word exposes what men suppose is safely hidden. The winking eye leaves no evidence among men, but the God who searches the heart reads the signal, and the sorrow it causes He will require.
webster_summary: To close and open the eye slyly, as a hint or signal of mischief between confederates; wickedness spoken without words.
webster_full: WINK, to shut and open the eye; and so to give a hint or signal by a motion of the eye.
From the Old English wincian, “to close the eyes.”
In Scripture it is the sign language of the wicked, who speak mischief without a word.
He winketh with his eyes, speaketh with his feet, teacheth with his fingers (Pro 6:13).
He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow (Pro 10:10).
scriptures: Pro 6:12
A naughty person, a wicked man, walketh with a froward mouth.
Pro 6:13
He winketh with his eyes, he speaketh with his feet, he teacheth with his fingers;
He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow: but a prating fool shall fall.
Let not them that are mine enemies wrongfully rejoice over me: neither let them wink with the eye that hate me without a cause.
corruption_summary: The old word names the sly signal of the conspirator; it recovers that God reads the wickedness which leaves no evidence among men.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live misuse here, and it is the sin that keeps its hands clean. The winking eye commits a man to nothing: no word is spoken, no promise given, nothing can be quoted back. It is the glance across the room, the raised brow, the knowing look that recruits an accomplice and leaves no trace. Our age has perfected it — the insinuation that can always be denied, the mockery that was only a joke, the malice that never quite said so. Solomon puts the winking eye in the same portrait as the froward mouth and the pointing finger, and the LORD names the whole company an abomination.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God judges the signal as surely as the speech. He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow, and the sorrow he causes is laid to his charge, though no man could swear to a word of it. David’s enemies hated him without a cause and winked in their triumph; the LORD saw the eye and heard the silence. Every member of the body is either an instrument of righteousness or an instrument of sin, and the man who has taught his eyes and feet and fingers to preach wickedness will answer for the sermon. What leaves no evidence in a court of men is written plainly before the throne.
roots_summary: The word means to close the eye slyly as a signal of mischief between confederates.
roots_lines: Wink — Old English wincian, “to close the eyes, to blink.”
Winketh is the archaic third-person form kept in the KJV.
It denotes not a blink but a signal, wickedness hinted without a word.
The wicked man winks, speaks with his feet, and teaches with his fingers (Pro 6:13).
The winking eye causeth sorrow, and God requires it (Pro 10:10).
usage: He winketh with his eyes and teacheth with his fingers — every member enlisted in the mischief.
He that winketh with the eye causeth sorrow: the sly man and the loud fool both come to ruin.
Let them not wink with the eye that hate me without a cause — God reads the silent signal.

etymology: From the Old French vanter, from the Late Latin vanitare, “to speak vainly, to boast,” from vanus, “empty, vain”; hence to boast, to brag, to display oneself — literally, to make much of emptiness.
biblical_def: To vaunt is to boast, to brag, to set oneself forth — and the Latin root confesses the whole indictment, for vanus is empty: to vaunt is to make much of nothing. The word governs one of the great scenes of the Old Testament. The LORD said unto Gideon, “The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me” (Jdg 7:2). Thirty-two thousand were too many; God pared them to three hundred with pitchers and lamps, not because He needed fewer but because Israel needed to know who saved them. Divine arithmetic is always aimed at the boast: God will win the battle in a way that leaves no room for the creature to vaunt. Paul draws the same line over salvation itself: “Not of works, lest any man should boast” (Eph 2:9). Grace is designed against vaunting; election, effectual calling, and imputed righteousness leave the sinner with nothing to display but Christ. And in the great chapter of love the word becomes a portrait: “charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up” (1Co 13:4). Charity is the exact opposite of the vaunting spirit, for love looks outward while boasting looks in the glass. Solomon shuts the door on the last excuse: “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth” (Pro 27:1). The man who vaunts does not even own his next hour.
webster_summary: To boast; to brag; to make a vain display of oneself or one’s doings.
webster_full: VAUNT, to boast; to brag; to make a vain display of what one is or has done.
From the Latin vanus, “empty” — to vaunt is to make much of nothing.
God thinned Gideon’s army lest Israel vaunt themselves against Him (Jdg 7:2).
Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up (1Co 13:4).
Salvation is not of works, lest any man should boast (Eph 2:9).
scriptures: Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
Jdg 7:2
And the LORD said unto Gideon, The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me.
Eph 2:9
Not of works, lest any man should boast.
Pro 27:1
Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the age has made vaunting a discipline and calls it confidence; Scripture calls it making much of emptiness.
corruption_paragraphs: Here is a corruption fully alive, and it is taught now as a skill. The self must be presented, the brand built, the accomplishment displayed; the man who does not vaunt himself is told he will be passed over. Scripture answers with the etymology: vanus is empty, and to vaunt is to make a loud noise about nothing. Charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up — love looks outward at its object, while boasting stands before the glass and admires. And Solomon strips the boaster of even his ground: boast not thyself of to morrow, for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth. The man who vaunts is bragging about property he does not own.

The doctrine underneath is grace itself. God thinned Gideon’s thirty-two thousand to three hundred for one stated reason — lest Israel vaunt themselves against Him, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me. The LORD arranges His victories so that the creature cannot claim them. So it is in salvation: not of works, lest any man should boast. Election is not of foreseen merit, the call is effectual and not earned, the righteousness is imputed and not ours; every door by which a boast might enter is shut deliberately. He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord. The saint has everything and vaunts nothing, for he owns not one thing he did not receive.

roots_lines: Vaunt — Old French vanter, from Late Latin vanitare, “to speak vainly.”
From vanus, “empty, vain” — the boast is a noise about nothing.
It denotes bragging, the display of self and self's doings.
God spared Israel the vaunt by winning with three hundred (Jdg 7:2).
Charity vaunteth not itself; grace leaves no room to boast (1Co 13:4; Eph 2:9).

Not of works, lest any man should boast — grace is designed against the vaunt.

etymology: From the Middle Dutch and Low German praten, “to talk, to chatter”; hence to babble, to talk much and to no purpose — and in the KJV, to run on with words that wound.
biblical_def: To prate is to babble — to pour out words without weight, without wisdom, and often without truth. Solomon twice pins the phrase “a prating fool shall fall” (Pro 10:8; Pro 10:10), and both times he sets the babbler against the man who listens: “The wise in heart will receive commandments: but a prating fool shall fall.” The Hebrew behind it is literally a fool of lips. Wisdom takes in a commandment and holds its peace; folly is all mouth, and it does not merely stumble — the margin says it shall be beaten. The same chapter gives the rule: “In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin” (Pro 10:19); talk enough and you will sin, for the flood carries the filth with it. Ecclesiastes adds the sting: “Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better” (Ecc 10:11) — the man of the tongue is a serpent whose bite no charm restrains. But John shows prating at its worst, inside the church. Diotrephes, who loved the preeminence, is charged thus: “I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church” (3Jn 1:10). Here prating is not idle chatter but ambition with a tongue — malicious words against faithful men, and then excommunication for any who welcome them. The babble of a proud man in the assembly is never harmless; it costs the brethren their place.
webster_summary: Talking much and idly; babbling; running on with words of no weight, and often of malice.
webster_full: PRATE, to talk much and idly; to babble; to be loquacious to no purpose.
From the Low German praten, “to talk, to chatter.”
The Hebrew phrase is literally a fool of lips; such a fool shall fall (Pro 10:8).
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin (Pro 10:19).
Diotrephes prated against the apostles with malicious words (3Jn 1:10).
scriptures: If I come, I will remember his deeds which he doeth, prating against us with malicious words: and not content therewith, neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church.
Pro 10:8
The wise in heart will receive commandments: but a prating fool shall fall.
In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise.
Surely the serpent will bite without enchantment; and a babbler is no better.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the endless religious quarrel online is Diotrephes with a wider room, prating against the brethren with malicious words.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is real and it is ours. Diotrephes loved the preeminence and prated against the apostles with malicious words — and the age has handed every Diotrephes a pulpit the size of the world. The endless religious quarrel that runs day and night, the professing Christian who has more zeal for the reply than for the commandment, the man who cannot receive an instruction but can compose a thousand words against a brother by noon — this is prating, and Scripture does not treat it as a harmless hobby. In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin. Talk long enough and you will sin; talk long enough about the brethren and you will sin against them.

Mark what John says prating leads to. Diotrephes did not stop with the malicious words: “neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and forbiddeth them that would, and casteth them out of the church.” The tongue that runs against faithful men soon takes up the keys and shuts the door on them. Solomon’s picture is exact: the wise in heart will receive commandments, but a prating fool shall fall — and the margin says he shall be beaten. The babbler is a serpent that bites without enchantment; no charm restrains him, and no one is safe. He that refraineth his lips is wise, and the church that prizes a quiet, teachable, commandment-receiving man over a clever mouth is wiser still.

Diotrephes prated against the apostles and cast out the brethren (3Jn 1:10).
usage: The wise in heart receive commandments; the prating fool has no room in his mouth for one.

In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin — the flood carries the filth along with it.

etymology: From the Old French jangler, “to chatter, to quarrel, to gossip”; hence wrangling, discordant talk — the word carries the sound of a bell struck out of tune, noise where music should be.
biblical_def: Jangling is wrangling — discordant, quarrelsome talk, the noise of men disputing to no end. The word itself sounds like a bell struck badly, and that is the point: where the doctrine of God should ring clear, there is only clatter. Paul charges Timothy against it at the outset: the end of the commandment is charity out of a pure heart, and a good conscience, and faith unfeigned, “from which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling” (1Ti 1:6). Mark the order — they did not begin as janglers; they swerved. Men leave the aim of love and a clean conscience, and having lost the mark they must do something with their religion, so they wrangle. Paul names them exactly: “Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm” (1Ti 1:7). The jangler is confident and ignorant at once, ambitious to teach and unable to explain. The charge is repeated at the end of the epistle: “keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called” (1Ti 6:20), and again to Timothy’s successor-charge, “charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers” (2Ti 2:14). Word-striving is never neutral. It profits nothing and it subverts the hearers — it pulls down the very people it was supposed to instruct. The remedy is not silence but the trust: keep the deposit, preach the commandment, and let the jangling alone.
webster_summary: Wrangling; quarrelsome, discordant talk; disputing about words to no profit.
webster_full: JANGLE, to quarrel in words; to wrangle; to sound discordantly, as an untuned bell.
From the Old French jangler, “to chatter, to quarrel.”
Vain jangling is the empty word-strife of those who have swerved from charity (1Ti 1:6).
The jangler desires to be a teacher of the law and understands neither what he says nor whereof he affirms (1Ti 1:7).
Striving about words profits nothing and subverts the hearers (2Ti 2:14).
scriptures: From which some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling;
Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the endless online religious quarrel is vain jangling with a larger congregation — confident, ignorant, and subverting the hearers.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is not in the word, which needs no defending, but in a practice our age has industrialized. Vain jangling now runs continuously: the professing Christian whose whole religion is the argument, who desires to be a teacher of the law and understands neither what he says nor whereof he affirms, who has an opinion on every controversy and charity out of a pure heart on none. Paul’s diagnosis is precise and unflattering — such men swerved. They left the end of the commandment, which is love from a clean conscience and faith unfeigned, and having abandoned the aim they kept the vocabulary, and the vocabulary went sour into noise. A bell out of tune still rings; that is the trouble.

The apostle will not let this pass as a harmless pastime. Striving about words is “to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers” — it does not merely fail to build, it pulls down; the onlookers are the casualties. And the janglers are always sure of themselves; confidence and ignorance keep close company. The remedy Paul gives is not a vow of silence but a deposit to guard: “keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called.” A man with a trust to keep has no time to jangle. Contend earnestly for the faith once delivered — that is commanded; wrangle about words for the pleasure of wrangling — that is forbidden, and the difference is the pure heart.
roots_summary: The word means wrangling, quarrelsome and discordant talk, disputing to no profit.
roots_lines: Jangle — Old French jangler, “to chatter, to quarrel, to gossip.”
It carries the sound of a bell struck out of tune — noise where music should be.
Vain jangling is what men turn aside to when they swerve from charity (1Ti 1:6).
The jangler would teach the law and understands neither what he says nor whereof he affirms.
Word-strife profits nothing and subverts the hearers (2Ti 2:14).
usage: Some having swerved have turned aside unto vain jangling — the noise begins where the aim was lost.
The jangler desires to teach the law and understands neither what he says nor whereof he affirms.
Keep that which is committed to thy trust: a man with a deposit to guard has no time to jangle.

etymology: A frequentative of scrape, kin to the Dutch schrabbelen, “to scratch repeatedly”; hence to scratch or claw with the hands, to make aimless marks — a KJV hapax, occurring but once, of David feigning madness at the gate of Gath.
biblical_def: To scrabble is to scratch and claw with the fingers, to make idiot marks on a surface. It occurs but once in all Scripture, and the scene is one of the strangest in the life of David. Fleeing Saul, he came to Achish king of Gath — to the very city of Goliath, with Goliath’s sword at his side — and “David laid up these words in his heart, and was sore afraid of Achish the king of Gath” (1Sa 21:12). So the anointed of the LORD, the man after God’s own heart, the giant-killer, “changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard” (1Sa 21:13). He clawed at the gateposts like a lunatic and drooled into his beard, and Achish said in contempt, “Have I need of mad men, that ye have brought this fellow to play the mad man in my presence?” (1Sa 21:15). Scripture does not flatter its saints. It records the scrabbling — the fear, the cowardice, the shabby deceit — because the Bible is not a book of heroes but a book of grace. And yet God preserved him. David escaped to the cave Adullam, and out of that cave came the psalms of a man who learned in Gath what he could not learn in triumph: “I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears” (Psa 34:4). The scrabbling hand of a frightened man was held by a providence he had forgotten to trust.
webster_summary: To scratch or claw with the hands; to make aimless marks; used once, of David feigning madness at the gate of Gath.
webster_full: SCRABBLE, to scratch or scrape with the hands; to make irregular, aimless marks.
A frequentative of scrape, kin to the Dutch schrabbelen, “to scratch repeatedly.”
A KJV hapax, occurring but once (1Sa 21:13). The margin reads “made marks.”
David scrabbled on the doors of the gate, feigning madness before Achish.
It marks the fear of a saint, honestly recorded and sovereignly overruled.
scriptures: And he changed his behaviour before them, and feigned himself mad in their hands, and scrabbled on the doors of the gate, and let his spittle fall down upon his beard.
And David laid up these words in his heart, and was sore afraid of Achish the king of Gath.
Have I need of mad men, that ye have brought this fellow to play the mad man in my presence? shall this fellow come into my house?
Psa 34:4
I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears.
corruption_summary: A single strange word for clawing at a gate; it recovers the honesty of Scripture, which records its saints’ cowardice and magnifies the grace that kept them.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a live misuse here, though it lies in how we read rather than in what the word means. Men handle the Bible as a gallery of heroes and then measure themselves against the portraits and despair, or else they flatten David into a moral example and quietly leave the gate of Gath out of the sermon. But the Holy Ghost wrote down the scrabbling. The giant-killer was sore afraid of a Philistine king, clawed at the doorposts like a lunatic, and let his spittle run into his beard, and the pagan sneered, Have I need of mad men? Scripture does not airbrush its saints, because Scripture is not commending them; it is commending their God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the grace which keeps us is not proportioned to the dignity of our conduct. David’s deliverance from Gath was no reward for a clever ruse; it was providence overruling a shabby one. He came out of that gate to the cave Adullam, and out of Adullam came the songs of a man who had learned what victory never taught him: I sought the LORD, and he heard me, and delivered me from all my fears. Perseverance is God’s work, not the saint’s performance. The hand that scrabbled on the doors was held all the while by the hand that had anointed it, and the same hand holds every believer who has been more afraid than faithful.
roots_summary: The word means to scratch or claw with the hands, to make aimless marks.
roots_lines: Scrabble — a frequentative of scrape, “to scratch again and again.”
Kin to the Dutch schrabbelen, “to scratch repeatedly.”
A KJV hapax, occurring but once in Scripture (1Sa 21:13).
David scrabbled on the doors of the gate, feigning madness before Achish.
It marks the fear of a saint whom sovereign grace preserved notwithstanding.
usage: David scrabbled on the doors of the gate — the giant-killer clawing at a wall in fear.
Achish sneered, Have I need of mad men? and the anointed of the LORD walked out alive.
Scripture records the scrabbling because it commends not the saint but the God who kept him.

etymology: From the Old French mincier, “to cut small,” from a Late Latin minutiare, from minutus, “small”; hence to walk with short, affected, dainty steps — the margin of the KJV reads “tripping nicely.”
biblical_def: To mince is to walk with short, affected steps — the studied, dainty gait of a woman on display. The word appears once, in Isaiah’s indictment of the daughters of Zion: “Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet” (Isa 3:16). Every clause is a posture. The neck is stretched out, the eyes deceive as they glance, the steps are cut small and studied, and ankle-chains chime at every pace so that no one may fail to notice her coming. This is not beauty; it is advertisement, and the LORD reads it as haughtiness, the heart’s pride worked out into a walk. The judgment answers the sin exactly. “Therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will discover their secret parts” (Isa 3:17); and He goes on to strip away the whole inventory — “the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon” (Isa 3:18) — ornament by ornament, for twenty verses. What was flaunted is uncovered; what was displayed is taken away. Against the mincing walk Scripture sets the apostolic order for godly women: “that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array” (1Ti 2:9). The daughters of Zion made an ornament of themselves; the daughters of the King are adorned with the fear of the LORD, and that beauty judgment cannot strip away.
webster_summary: Walking with short, affected, dainty steps; the studied gait of display — the KJV margin, “tripping nicely.”
webster_full: MINCE, to walk with short steps; to affect a dainty, studied gait.
From the Old French mincier, “to cut small” — the steps are cut short.
The KJV margin at Isa 3:16 reads “tripping nicely.”
The daughters of Zion walked mincing, with stretched necks and tinkling feet.
Isaiah names the gait haughtiness, and the LORD strips away the finery that fed it (Isa 3:18).
scriptures: Isa 3:16
Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:
Isa 3:17
Therefore the Lord will smite with a scab the crown of the head of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will discover their secret parts.
Isa 3:18
In that day the Lord will take away the bravery of their tinkling ornaments about their feet, and their cauls, and their round tires like the moon,
In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the mincing walk of Zion is now a whole industry of self-display, and Scripture still names the gait haughtiness.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is fully alive, and it has been given cameras. Isaiah’s daughters of Zion had stretched necks, wanton eyes, cut and studied steps, and ankle-bells to announce their approach; ours have the same heart and better instruments. The gait is the doctrine: display is not modesty, and the LORD does not read the mincing walk as beauty but as haughtiness — pride worked outward until the body preaches it. And the sin is not in being fair. Isaiah is not against ornament as such; he is against the woman who has made an ornament of herself, and against the men of a city who let her, for the same chapter arraigns Zion’s failed rulers in the very next breath.

The judgment fits the crime with terrible precision. She uncovered herself to be seen, and “the LORD will discover their secret parts”; she flaunted the finery, and the LORD takes away the bravery of the tinkling ornaments, the cauls, the round tires like the moon — twenty verses of inventory, stripped item by item, until the perfume is stench and the girdle a rent. What a woman displays she will lose. Against this Paul sets the order that endures: modest apparel, shamefacedness, sobriety, and good works becoming women professing godliness. Favour is deceitful and beauty is vain, but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised — and that adorning no day of visitation can strip away.
roots_summary: The word means to walk with short, affected, dainty steps — the gait of display.
roots_lines: Mince — Old French mincier, “to cut small,” from Latin minutus.
The steps are cut short and studied; the KJV margin reads “tripping nicely.”
It denotes an affected, advertising gait, not a natural one.
The daughters of Zion walked mincing, with stretched necks and tinkling feet (Isa 3:16).
The LORD names the walk haughtiness and strips away its ornaments (Isa 3:18).
usage: Walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet — the gait was the advertisement.
The LORD reads the mincing step as haughtiness: pride worked outward till the body preaches it.
What Zion’s daughters displayed, the day of visitation stripped away, ornament by ornament.

etymology: The archaic third-person form of list, from the Old English lystan, “to please, to desire” (kin to lust); hence to please oneself, to will, to choose — to do a thing because one wills it and for no cause outside oneself.
biblical_def: To list is to please, to will, to choose — to act from one’s own good pleasure and no other cause. The word is rare in the KJV and one of its two occurrences carries a doctrine the church has fought over ever since. Our Lord tells Nicodemus, “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit” (Joh 3:8). The comparison is not loose. In the Greek one word serves for both wind and Spirit, and the point of likeness is stated plainly: the wind blows where it wills. It asks no leave of the field it crosses. You hear its sound — the effects are unmistakable — but you did not summon it, cannot direct it, and cannot tell whence it came. So is every one that is born of the Spirit. The new birth is the Spirit’s sovereign act, worked where He pleases, and the man born again can no more account for the wind that blew upon him than Nicodemus could. James uses the word of a ship’s helm, turned “whithersoever the governor listeth” (Jas 3:4) — the same sense: the governor’s will decides, not the ship’s. This is the whole of monergism in a single archaic verb. They “were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” (Joh 1:13); and “as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom he will” (Joh 5:21).
webster_summary: To please; to desire; to choose — to act of one’s own will, as the wind that bloweth where it listeth.
webster_full: LIST, to be disposed; to please; to choose; to will.
From the Old English lystan, “to please, to desire,” kin to lust.
Listeth is the archaic third-person form kept in the KJV.
The wind bloweth where it listeth — it asks no leave (Joh 3:8).
The helm turns whithersoever the governor listeth: the will that decides is his (Jas 3:4).
scriptures: Joh 3:8
The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
Jas 3:4
Behold also the ships, which though they be so great, and are driven of fierce winds, yet are they turned about with a very small helm, whithersoever the governor listeth.
Joh 1:13
Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
Joh 5:21
For as the Father raiseth up the dead, and quickeneth them; even so the Son quickeneth whom he will.
corruption_summary: A live corruption: the Arminian reading softens Joh 3:8 into the freedom of the sinner, when Christ said the wind — the Spirit — bloweth where it listeth.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is old and it is doctrinal. The Arminian softening of Joh 3:8 turns the verse inside out: the freedom in the text is made the sinner’s freedom — the mysterious, unpredictable, uncontainable human response — and the Spirit is left standing at the door of a will He may not enter. But read the sentence. It is the wind that bloweth where it listeth; it is the wind whose sound you hear and whose origin you cannot trace; and Christ says so is every one that is born of the Spirit. The one whose will decides is not Nicodemus. The Greek uses one word for wind and Spirit precisely so the figure cannot be prised apart. To make the sovereign One in this verse the creature is to reverse the very sentence spoken to teach a master of Israel that he must be born from above.

Set the surrounding texts beside it and the case is closed. Men are “born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God” — three denials, and the third is the decisive one: not of the will of man. “Even so the Son quickeneth whom he will.” And James, using the same verb of a helm, shows the plain sense: the ship goes whithersoever the governor listeth, not whithersoever the ship prefers. Regeneration is monergistic; the dead do not co-operate in their raising. This is no cold doctrine but the sinner’s only hope, for if the new birth waited on the will of the flesh it would wait for ever. The wind blew on us who could not summon it, and that is why we are here.

It denotes acting from one's own will, with no cause outside oneself.
The wind bloweth where it listeth — so is every one born of the Spirit (Joh 3:8).
The helm turns whithersoever the governor listeth, not whither the ship prefers (Jas 3:4).

Thou hearest the sound thereof — the new birth is unmistakable in effect and untraceable in origin.
Whithersoever the governor listeth: the helm goes where the will that holds it decides.
